questions.question: Young modulus from a small extension and wire-diameter uncertainty
questions.subtopic: RP4 Young modulus and propagated diameter uncertainty
questions.prompt: A wire has length (1.200 ± 0.005) m, diameter (0.300 ± 0.005) mm and extension (2.00 ± 0.05) mm when force (6.0 ± 0.1) N is applied. Assume Hooke's law applies and the wire is cylindrical. (a) Convert the diameter and extension to SI units and determine cross-sectional area. (b) Calculate the Young modulus E in Pa and GPa. (c) Find the percentage uncertainty in E using the standard uncertainty rules for products, quotients and powers; give E with an appropriate absolute uncertainty. (d) Explain why the diameter's percentage uncertainty is doubled, not added once. [9 marks]
markPoints: The diameter is 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m, the extension is 2.00 × 10⁻³ m.
Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 7.07 × 10⁻⁸ m².
Young modulus E = F L/(A ΔL).
This is approximately 50.9 GPa.
Percentage uncertainties are force 1.67%, length 0.417%, diameter 1.67% and extension 2.50%.
Since E is proportional to F L d⁻²(ΔL)⁻¹, total estimated uncertainty = 1.67 + 0.417 + 2(1.67) + 2.50 = 7.92%.
The absolute uncertainty is 0.0792 × 50.9 ≈ 4.0 GPa, so E ≈ (51 ± 4) GPa.
The exponent −2 on diameter means its fractional uncertainty has twice the effect on E; using just 1.67% for diameter understates uncertainty.
questions.modelAnswer: The diameter is 3.00 × 10⁻⁴ m, the extension is 2.00 × 10⁻³ m. Cross-sectional area A = πd²/4 = 7.07 × 10⁻⁸ m². Young modulus E = F L/(A ΔL). E = (6.0 × 1.200)/(7.0686 × 10⁻⁸ × 0.00200) = 5.09 × 10¹⁰ Pa. This is approximately 50.9 GPa. Percentage uncertainties are force 1.67%, length 0.417%, diameter 1.67% and extension 2.50%. Since E is proportional to F L d⁻²(ΔL)⁻¹, total estimated uncertainty = 1.67 + 0.417 + 2(1.67) + 2.50 = 7.92%. The absolute uncertainty is 0.0792 × 50.9 ≈ 4.0 GPa, so E ≈ (51 ± 4) GPa. The exponent −2 on diameter means its fractional uncertainty has twice the effect on E; using just 1.67% for diameter understates uncertainty.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Measurement and Particle Reasoning
questions.question: Emf and internal resistance from a voltage–current graph with uncertainty
questions.subtopic: RP6 best-fit, extreme gradients and intercepts
questions.prompt: For an idealised cell, the best-fit terminal-p.d. graph V (vertical axis) against I (horizontal axis) passes through (0.20 A, 1.44 V) and (1.00 A, 0.80 V). Plausible steepest and shallowest lines through the error bars have gradients −0.90 Ω and −0.70 Ω. Corresponding extreme intercepts are 1.72 V and 1.48 V. (a) Determine the best-fit gradient and y-intercept. (b) Identify emf and internal resistance from the equation V = ε − Ir. (c) Determine approximate absolute uncertainties in gradient, internal resistance and emf using the half-range method. (d) State why the line should not be forced through the origin and how error bars help judge a proposed model. [8 marks]
markPoints: The best-fit gradient is (0.80 − 1.44)/(1.00 − 0.20) = −0.80 V A⁻¹.
Using V = ε − Ir, the graph gradient equals −r.
Thus the internal resistance is r = +0.80 Ω.
Extrapolating the best-fit line to I = 0 gives emf ε = V + Ir = 1.44 + 0.80 × 0.20 = 1.60 V.
Half the difference between extreme gradients gives gradient uncertainty (0.90 − 0.70)/2 = 0.10 Ω.
So internal resistance is approximately (0.80 ± 0.10) Ω.
Half the extreme intercept range gives emf uncertainty (1.72 − 1.48)/2 = 0.12 V; emf ≈ (1.60 ± 0.12) V.
The terminal voltage at zero current equals nonzero emf; forcing the line through the origin is physically wrong, and error bars show whether lines are consistent with observations.
questions.modelAnswer: The best-fit gradient is (0.80 − 1.44)/(1.00 − 0.20) = −0.80 V A⁻¹. Using V = ε − Ir, the graph gradient equals −r. Thus the internal resistance is r = +0.80 Ω. Extrapolating the best-fit line to I = 0 gives emf ε = V + Ir = 1.44 + 0.80 × 0.20 = 1.60 V. Half the difference between extreme gradients gives gradient uncertainty (0.90 − 0.70)/2 = 0.10 Ω. So internal resistance is approximately (0.80 ± 0.10) Ω. Half the extreme intercept range gives emf uncertainty (1.72 − 1.48)/2 = 0.12 V; emf ≈ (1.60 ± 0.12) V. The terminal voltage at zero current equals nonzero emf; forcing the line through the origin is physically wrong, and error bars show whether lines are consistent with observations.

6: The uncertainty in emf is 0.12 V

questions.question: Resistivity and uncertainty using diameter and V–I readings
questions.subtopic: RP5 resistivity with instrument uncertainty and power
questions.prompt: A wire used in a resistivity calculation has length (1.50 ± 0.01) m and measured diameter (0.400 ± 0.005) mm. At one operating point the measured p.d. is (2.40 ± 0.02) V and current is (0.600 ± 0.010) A. Assume a uniform cylindrical wire and ohmic behaviour at constant temperature. (a) Calculate resistance. (b) Calculate cross-sectional area and resistivity. (c) Calculate approximate percentage uncertainty in resistivity, using the uncertainties in all four measured quantities. (d) Give the result with an absolute uncertainty and explain why temperature control matters. [8 marks]
markPoints: Resistance R = V/I = 2.40/0.600 = 4.00 Ω.
Diameter 0.400 mm = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Area A = πd²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m².
Percentage uncertainties in V and I are 0.833% and 1.67%, contributing 2.50% in resistance.
Diameter contributes twice its 1.25% uncertainty because area ∝ d², giving 2.50% in area.
Length contributes 0.667%, so total resistivity percentage uncertainty ≈ 0.833 + 1.67 + 2.50 + 0.667 = 5.67%, or about ±1.9 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
A suitable final result is (3.35 ± 0.19) × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; temperature must be controlled because resistance and resistivity usually vary with temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Resistance R = V/I = 2.40/0.600 = 4.00 Ω. Diameter 0.400 mm = 4.00 × 10⁻⁴ m. Area A = πd²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m². Resistivity ρ = RA/L = (4.00 × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁷)/1.50 = 3.35 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. Percentage uncertainties in V and I are 0.833% and 1.67%, contributing 2.50% in resistance. Diameter contributes twice its 1.25% uncertainty because area ∝ d², giving 2.50% in area. Length contributes 0.667%, so total resistivity percentage uncertainty ≈ 0.833 + 1.67 + 2.50 + 0.667 = 5.67%, or about ±1.9 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. A suitable final result is (3.35 ± 0.19) × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; temperature must be controlled because resistance and resistivity usually vary with temperature.

questions.question: Distance from two positions, uncertainty and systematic offsets
questions.subtopic: Different readings, distance uncertainties and derived speed
questions.prompt: A moving object passes two marks. Its recorded positions are (0.24 ± 0.01) m and (1.44 ± 0.01) m, and the elapsed time is (0.600 ± 0.005) s. (a) Calculate the displacement and its absolute uncertainty using the standard rule for subtraction. (b) Calculate average velocity and its percentage uncertainty, giving a suitable final result. (c) Explain why subtracting two readings may remove a constant zero offset without eliminating every systematic error. [7 marks]
markPoints: Displacement Δx = 1.44 − 0.24 = 1.20 m.
For subtraction, absolute uncertainties add: ±0.01 + ±0.01 = ±0.02 m.
Percentage uncertainty in displacement = 0.02/1.20 × 100 = 1.67%.
Average velocity v = 1.20/0.600 = 2.00 m s⁻¹.
Time percentage uncertainty = 0.005/0.600 × 100 = 0.833%.
Total percentage uncertainty in velocity for the quotient is ≈ 1.67 + 0.833 = 2.50%, or ±0.050 m s⁻¹; v = (2.00 ± 0.05) m s⁻¹.
The same constant zero offset cancels when taking two positions' difference, but scale-calibration errors or changing offsets may remain.
questions.modelAnswer: Displacement Δx = 1.44 − 0.24 = 1.20 m. For subtraction, absolute uncertainties add: ±0.01 + ±0.01 = ±0.02 m. Percentage uncertainty in displacement = 0.02/1.20 × 100 = 1.67%. Average velocity v = 1.20/0.600 = 2.00 m s⁻¹. Time percentage uncertainty = 0.005/0.600 × 100 = 0.833%. Total percentage uncertainty in velocity for the quotient is ≈ 1.67 + 0.833 = 2.50%, or ±0.050 m s⁻¹; v = (2.00 ± 0.05) m s⁻¹. The same constant zero offset cancels when taking two positions' difference, but scale-calibration errors or changing offsets may remain.

questions.question: Order-of-magnitude photon count from electricity energy
questions.subtopic: SI conversion, photon energy and order of magnitude
questions.prompt: For a theoretical energy comparison, a device transfers 2.20 kW h of energy. Suppose, unrealistically, that all this energy is converted into monochromatic 400 nm photons. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. (a) Convert the device energy to joules. (b) Find the energy of one photon in joules and eV. (c) Calculate the approximate number of photons and give its nearest power of ten. (d) State why the photon-count result is only a model estimate. [8 marks]
markPoints: One kW h = 3.60 × 10⁶ J.
The total energy is 2.20 × 3.60 × 10⁶ = 7.92 × 10⁶ J.
In electronvolts E ≈ (4.9725 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3.11 eV.
Number of photons N = 7.92 × 10⁶/(4.9725 × 10⁻¹⁹).
Thus N ≈ 1.59 × 10²⁵, nearest order of magnitude 10²⁵.
The estimate assumes perfect conversion of all transferred energy into identical-wavelength photons; real losses invalidate that ideal assumption.
questions.modelAnswer: One kW h = 3.60 × 10⁶ J. The total energy is 2.20 × 3.60 × 10⁶ = 7.92 × 10⁶ J. 400 nm = 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ m. Photon energy E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(4.00 × 10⁻⁷) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. In electronvolts E ≈ (4.9725 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3.11 eV. Number of photons N = 7.92 × 10⁶/(4.9725 × 10⁻¹⁹). Thus N ≈ 1.59 × 10²⁵, nearest order of magnitude 10²⁵. The estimate assumes perfect conversion of all transferred energy into identical-wavelength photons; real losses invalidate that ideal assumption.

questions.question: Complete two beta-decay equations using conservation rules
questions.subtopic: Conservation of electron-family lepton number in beta decay
questions.prompt: In these written, hypothetical nuclear-transformation equations, fill missing particles: (a) ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ___ + ___; (b) ²²₁₁Na → ²²₁₀Ne + ___ + ___. Use β⁻ and β⁺ emission, respectively. (c) State the changes in quark flavour inside a nucleon for each decay. (d) Justify the identities of the associated neutrinos using charge and electron-family lepton-number conservation. [8 marks]
markPoints: For ¹⁴₆C beta-minus decay, an electron e⁻ (β⁻) is emitted.
The other emitted particle in beta-minus decay is an electron antineutrino, anti-νₑ.
Beta-minus decay changes a down quark to an up quark inside the neutron, converting n to p.
In ²²₁₁Na beta-plus decay, a positron e⁺ (β⁺) is emitted.
The other emitted particle in beta-plus decay is an electron neutrino, νₑ.
Beta-plus decay changes an up quark to a down quark inside the proton, converting p to n.
Electric charge and nucleon/baryon number remain conserved in both transformations.
Electron-family lepton number is conserved: e⁻ (+1) pairs with anti-νₑ (−1), and e⁺ (−1) pairs with νₑ (+1).
questions.modelAnswer: For ¹⁴₆C beta-minus decay, an electron e⁻ (β⁻) is emitted. The other emitted particle in beta-minus decay is an electron antineutrino, anti-νₑ. Beta-minus decay changes a down quark to an up quark inside the neutron, converting n to p. In ²²₁₁Na beta-plus decay, a positron e⁺ (β⁺) is emitted. The other emitted particle in beta-plus decay is an electron neutrino, νₑ. Beta-plus decay changes an up quark to a down quark inside the proton, converting p to n. Electric charge and nucleon/baryon number remain conserved in both transformations. Electron-family lepton number is conserved: e⁻ (+1) pairs with anti-νₑ (−1), and e⁺ (−1) pairs with νₑ (+1).

questions.question: Identify strong or weak interactions from strangeness changes
questions.subtopic: Strangeness in strong production and weak decay with supplied new particle
questions.prompt: For a theoretical particle-collision exercise, you are given: proton p has charge +1, baryon number +1 and strangeness 0; π⁻ has charge −1, baryon number 0 and strangeness 0; K⁰ has charge 0, baryon number 0 and strangeness +1; neutral Λ has charge 0, baryon number +1 and strangeness −1; pions have strangeness 0. (a) Assess π⁻ + p → K⁰ + Λ for charge, baryon number and total strangeness conservation. (b) Explain why this reaction can occur by the strong interaction despite producing strange particles. (c) For K⁰ → π⁺ + π⁻, compare strangeness before and after and identify the class of interaction. [8 marks]
markPoints: Incoming charge is (−1) + (+1) = 0 and outgoing charge is 0 + 0 = 0.
Incoming baryon number is 0 + 1 = 1 and outgoing is 0 + 1 = 1.
Incoming total strangeness is 0 + 0 = 0.
Outgoing total strangeness is +1 + (−1) = 0.
The reaction conserves charge, baryon number and strangeness, so strong production is allowed by these rules.
The produced strange particles carry opposite strangeness, so they can be produced together while net strangeness remains zero.
For K⁰ → π⁺ + π⁻, initial strangeness +1 becomes 0, a change of −1.
Since strangeness changes by one unit, this kaon decay proceeds through the weak interaction rather than the strong interaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Incoming charge is (−1) + (+1) = 0 and outgoing charge is 0 + 0 = 0. Incoming baryon number is 0 + 1 = 1 and outgoing is 0 + 1 = 1. Incoming total strangeness is 0 + 0 = 0. Outgoing total strangeness is +1 + (−1) = 0. The reaction conserves charge, baryon number and strangeness, so strong production is allowed by these rules. The produced strange particles carry opposite strangeness, so they can be produced together while net strangeness remains zero. For K⁰ → π⁺ + π⁻, initial strangeness +1 becomes 0, a change of −1. Since strangeness changes by one unit, this kaon decay proceeds through the weak interaction rather than the strong interaction.

questions.series: Original AQA-style Measurement and Particle Reasoning
questions.question: Photon wavelength after annihilation and excess pair-production energy
questions.subtopic: Annihilation, photon energies and pair production threshold
questions.prompt: A slow electron and slow positron annihilate at rest and produce two equal-energy gamma photons. Electron/positron rest energy is 0.511 MeV each. Separately, a 1.50 MeV photon produces an electron–positron pair near a nucleus. Use 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. (a) Explain why the initial annihilation produces two opposed photons. (b) Find energy of each in MeV and joules, then wavelength. (c) Give the minimum rest-energy requirement for pair creation and the remaining kinetic energy shared between created particles in the 1.50 MeV case, neglecting nuclear recoil. (d) Explain the role of the nearby nucleus. [8 marks]
markPoints: A nearly stationary electron–positron pair has close to zero initial momentum; two photons in opposite directions conserve momentum.
The total rest energy is 2 × 0.511 = 1.022 MeV.
Each annihilation photon therefore has energy 0.511 MeV.
Using λ = hc/E gives photon wavelength ≈ 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m.
An electron–positron pair requires at least 1.022 MeV of rest energy.
For a 1.50 MeV incident photon, remaining energy is approximately 1.50 − 1.022 = 0.478 MeV as particle kinetic energy (neglect nuclear recoil).
The nearby nucleus takes recoil momentum so both energy and momentum can be conserved during single-photon pair production.
questions.modelAnswer: A nearly stationary electron–positron pair has close to zero initial momentum; two photons in opposite directions conserve momentum. The total rest energy is 2 × 0.511 = 1.022 MeV. Each annihilation photon therefore has energy 0.511 MeV. 0.511 MeV equals 0.511 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. Using λ = hc/E gives photon wavelength ≈ 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m. An electron–positron pair requires at least 1.022 MeV of rest energy. For a 1.50 MeV incident photon, remaining energy is approximately 1.50 − 1.022 = 0.478 MeV as particle kinetic energy (neglect nuclear recoil). The nearby nucleus takes recoil momentum so both energy and momentum can be conserved during single-photon pair production.

2: The energy of one photon is 0.511 MeV
6: The excess kinetic energy is 0.478 MeV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Measurement and Particle Reasoning
questions.question: Connect a level transition to photoelectron kinetic energy
questions.subtopic: Photon emission from atomic levels and photoelectric response
questions.prompt: An atom has allowed electron levels −6.00 eV, −2.00 eV and −1.00 eV, with 0 eV the ionisation limit. The atom emits a photon in the transition from −2.00 eV to −6.00 eV. That photon illuminates a metal of work function 2.30 eV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. (a) Find photon energy in eV and joules. (b) Calculate its wavelength. (c) Determine maximum photoelectron kinetic energy and stopping potential. (d) Predict effects on maximum kinetic energy and electron emission rate if photon intensity doubles at unchanged wavelength above threshold. [8 marks]
markPoints: The emitted photon energy equals the drop  (−2.00) − (−6.00) = 4.00 eV.
In joules this is 4.00 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Photon wavelength λ = hc/E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 3.11 × 10⁻⁷ m.
The photon energy exceeds the work function of 2.30 eV so emission is possible.
Maximum photoelectron kinetic energy is Ek(max) = 4.00 − 2.30 = 1.70 eV.
In the stopping-potential relation eVs = Ek(max), Vs = 1.70 V.
Doubling light intensity at the same frequency does not alter photon energy or maximum photoelectron kinetic energy.
With sufficient incident photons and unchanged experimental conditions, the photoelectron emission rate increases.
questions.modelAnswer: The emitted photon energy equals the drop  (−2.00) − (−6.00) = 4.00 eV. In joules this is 4.00 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photon wavelength λ = hc/E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(6.40 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 3.11 × 10⁻⁷ m. The photon energy exceeds the work function of 2.30 eV so emission is possible. Maximum photoelectron kinetic energy is Ek(max) = 4.00 − 2.30 = 1.70 eV. In the stopping-potential relation eVs = Ek(max), Vs = 1.70 V. Doubling light intensity at the same frequency does not alter photon energy or maximum photoelectron kinetic energy. With sufficient incident photons and unchanged experimental conditions, the photoelectron emission rate increases.

questions.question: Electron matter wavelength and the effect of quadrupling voltage
questions.subtopic: de Broglie wavelength and accelerating voltage
questions.prompt: An electron starts essentially at rest and is accelerated through an ideal potential difference of 200 V. Treat its final speed as non-relativistic. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. (a) Find electron kinetic energy, momentum and de Broglie wavelength. (b) State the new momentum and wavelength if the accelerating voltage is increased to 800 V. (c) Explain the trend in electron-diffraction spread as momentum increases. [7 marks]
markPoints: The electron gains kinetic energy Ek = eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 200 = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.
For non-relativistic motion, p = √(2mEk).
Substitution gives p ≈ √(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 7.64 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹.
De Broglie wavelength λ = h/p ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(7.64 × 10⁻²⁴) = 8.68 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
Quadrupling the accelerating voltage quadruples Ek but doubles momentum because p ∝ √Ek.
At 800 V the momentum becomes about 1.53 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ and wavelength halves to about 4.34 × 10⁻¹¹ m.
Shorter de Broglie wavelength at higher momentum means smaller electron-diffraction angles for a fixed lattice spacing.

Substitution gives p ≈ √(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 7.64 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. De Broglie wavelength λ = h/p ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(7.64 × 10⁻²⁴) = 8.68 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Quadrupling the accelerating voltage quadruples Ek but doubles momentum because p ∝ √Ek. At 800 V the momentum becomes about 1.53 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ and wavelength halves to about 4.34 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Shorter de Broglie wavelength at higher momentum means smaller electron-diffraction angles for a fixed lattice spacing.
